q: When we take a thin piece of magnetised steel bar and cut it into three smaller pieces, only the end pieces remain magnets.
e: False. Cut a magnet and every piece is a magnet, middle included, each with a north and a south. Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole, and like poles push apart.

q: Every piece of a cut magnetised steel bar is a magnet with a $N$-pole and $S$-pole.
e: True. Every piece of a cut magnetised steel bar is a magnet with a $N$-pole and $S$-pole. Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole, and like poles push apart.

q: We can suppose that the original magnet is made up of lots of magnets all lined up with their $N$-poles pointing in same direction.
e: True. We can suppose that the original magnet is made up of lots of magnets all lined up with their $N$-poles pointing in same direction. Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole, and like poles push apart.

q: This explains why the poles of the magnet are around the ends.
e: True. This explains why the poles of the magnet are around the ends. Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole, and like poles push apart.

q: In the case of unmagnetised bar, we can imagine the 'tiny' magnets pointing in random direction.
e: True. In the case of unmagnetised bar, we can imagine the 'tiny' magnets pointing in random direction. Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole, and like poles push apart.

q: In an unmagnetised bar, the resulting magnetic effect of all the tiny magnets is amplified.
e: False. In an unmagnetised bar the tiny magnets point every which way, so their effects cancel, they are not amplified. Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole, and like poles push apart.

q: Both the magnetised materials (inclusive of magnets) and unmagnetised materials are made up of tiny magnets.
e: True. Both the magnetised materials (inclusive of magnets) and unmagnetised materials are made up of tiny magnets. Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole, and like poles push apart.
